passage: In the college corridor, a group was passing round the class results when someone said, loudly enough for everyone, "Naveen, did you get your marks from a lucky draw?" A couple of people laughed. Naveen laughed too, a wide, quick smile, and said, "Yeah, best draw of my life." He walked on without looking at anyone. Suraj noticed the smile didn't reach his eyes and that Naveen's fingers tightened round his folder. He didn't rush over or say "I know you're hurt." He just sent a message that evening: "That joke earlier was rubbish. You okay? No need to reply now." A reply came an hour later: "Thanks. It stung a bit." Suraj wrote back, "I'm here."

qa.q: What did someone ask Naveen about his marks?
qa.a: Someone asked, 'Did you get your marks from a lucky draw?'

qa.q: What might Naveen have been feeling behind his wide, quick smile?
qa.a: Probably hurt and a wish not to look weak, though Suraj can't be sure, and Naveen later admitted it stung a bit.

qa.q: Why did Suraj follow up privately instead of in front of everyone?
qa.a: A public comment could make Naveen feel more exposed, while a private message let him reply in his own time without pressure.

qa.q: How might the people who laughed have seen the moment?
qa.a: They may have thought Naveen took the joke well, since he laughed too, and never realised it hurt.

grounding: A teen laughs off a hurtful joke to avoid looking weak, and a friend gently follows up privately.

"Payal, you laughed when Kavya said that about your accent."
"Everyone did."
"I know, but you laughed the loudest." Indu sat on the hostel bed and folded her arms. "I'm not saying you're upset. I just wondered."
Payal turned her phone over in her hands. "It's just a joke."
"Okay. If it was, then that's fine. If it wasn't, I don't mind hearing it either."
There was a long pause. "It stung a bit," Payal said, quietly. "But I didn't want to be the girl who can't take a joke."
"You're allowed to be both."
Payal smiled properly this time. "Thanks for asking me alone. Not in front of them."

qa.q: Where were Indu and Payal talking?
qa.a: They were talking on the hostel bed.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she laughed at the accent joke?
qa.a: She felt hurt, since it stung a bit, but she laughed to avoid looking like someone who can't take a joke.

qa.q: What did Indu do well when she raised the topic?
qa.a: She asked privately, didn't assume, and said Payal could tell her either way, which made it safe to speak.

qa.q: How might Kavya have felt about the joke?
qa.a: Kavya may not have known it hurt, since Payal laughed along, and Kavya might want to know in order to stop.

grounding: A teen smiles and laughs off a hurtful joke, and a friend follows up privately without assuming.

passage:
In Class 8, a boy in my class said, loudly, "Tanuja's mother cleans houses, so Tanuja must be good at mopping!" and mimed mopping the floor. Everyone laughed.
I laughed too. I even said, "Want me to do your house next?" More laughter. I smiled through the whole of maths.
Inside, I felt like I'd been punched. My mother works so hard. I was so ashamed that I'd laughed along.
Only Tenzin noticed. At the end of the day, by the cycle stand, away from everyone, Tenzin said, "That joke wasn't funny. Are you okay?"
I wanted to say "I'm fine" again. But Tenzin didn't assume anything, just waited.
So I said, "No. It really hurt."
Tenzin said, "I thought so. Your smile looked stuck." Then, "Do you want to tell Ma'am, or just walk home together today?"
We walked. The next day, I told Ma'am myself.

qa.q: What did the boy mime?
qa.a: The boy mimed mopping the floor.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling behind the smile?
qa.a: Tanuja felt deeply hurt, as if punched, and ashamed of having laughed along at a joke about Tanuja's hard-working mother.

qa.q: Which of Tenzin's choices helped?
qa.a: Tenzin followed up privately, didn't assume, waited for an answer, and offered choices of support.

qa.q: How did the class read Tanuja's laughing back?
qa.a: They probably thought Tanuja found the joke funny and didn't mind, missing the hurt behind the smile.

grounding: The account shows a teenager laughing off a hurtful joke to avoid looking weak, and a friend following up privately.

passage:
Counsellor's note - Binita, Class 10, Thursday
Rehana came to see me at lunch, sent by her class teacher. In PE, while the class changed shoes, a group of girls had joked about her old sports shoes: "Did you get them from your grandmother?" Rehana laughed loudly and made a joke back. The teacher, who knows her well, thought the laugh sounded forced.
With me, Rehana smiled for the first ten minutes. "It's fine. It was funny."
I didn't argue. I said, "Sometimes people laugh because it's easier than showing it hurt. If that's what happened, that's okay."
Her smile stayed, but her eyes filled up. "My father lost his job. We can't buy new ones this year. I didn't want them to know."
I told her it was not her fault, and that I'd make sure the PE teacher addressed the teasing without mentioning her family. She left looking lighter.

qa.q: What did the girls joke about?
qa.a: About her old sports shoes.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling behind her smile?
qa.a: Rehana felt hurt and ashamed about the family's money troubles, and laughed to avoid looking weak.

qa.q: How did Binita respond in a way that helped?
qa.a: She didn't argue or assume, gently allowed for hurt behind a laugh, and offered practical support without exposing Rehana's family.

qa.q: How might the girls who joked have read Rehana's laugh?
qa.a: They probably thought she was fine with it, since she laughed and joked back.

grounding: The counsellor's note shows a teenager smiling through a hurtful joke to protect herself, and a gentle private follow-up.

passage:
Monday
In the canteen line today, one of the seniors put his hand on Ujjwal's head and said, "Oh sorry, didn't see you down there, shorty!" Everyone laughed. Ujjwal laughed the loudest. He even stood on tiptoe and said, "Better?"
Everyone said, "Ujjwal is so funny."
But I saw him afterwards. He sat alone and didn't finish his rice. When his friends called him, he smiled, but only with his mouth.
I didn't want to assume, and I didn't want to embarrass him. So I waited till we were alone near the bus.
"The shorty thing. Was that okay, or not really?"
He looked at me for a long time. "Not really. It's every day."
"That's rubbish. You don't have to laugh."
"If I don't, it's worse."
I told him he could sit with me at lunch tomorrow, and that if he wanted, I'd go with him to Sir.
- Zainab

qa.q: What did the senior call Ujjwal?
qa.a: Shorty.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling behind his loud laugh?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt hurt and tired of daily teasing, but laughed to avoid looking weak and making it worse.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that was wise?
qa.a: Zainab waited until they were alone, asked gently without assuming, and offered company and support in telling Sir.

qa.q: How did the crowd in the canteen see Ujjwal?
qa.a: They saw him as funny and fine with it, not noticing the hurt behind his smile.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager laughing off a hurtful joke to avoid looking weak, and a friend following up privately with support.
